source.title: Leveraging large language models for the deidentification and temporal normalization of sensitive health information in electronic health records
source.authors: Hong-Jie Dai; T. H. Mir; Ching-Tai Chen; Chien-Chang Chen; Hao Yang; Chung-Hong Lee; Yi-Yun Chou; Yue Teng; Shalini Gupta; O. Panchal; Divyabharathy Ramesh Nadar; Wei-Hsiang Liao; Yu-Chuan Lin; Zixiang Zhao; Richard Tzong-Han Tsai; Yung-Chun Chang; Jitendra Jonnagaddala

record.file_problem: Whole article text is present. Supplementary materials are referenced but not included.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream task performance across model sizes and training approaches, using F1 rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit loss power laws, extrapolate loss from small runs, or evaluate compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its scale comparisons bear on V6 only. Values in the performance plots are not transcribed numerically in the text; rows relying on those values are marked figure only.
record.test_reason: It compares downstream deidentification and temporal-normalization F1 across the Pythia suite (70M–12B) under ICL and fine-tuning. That is a new clinical task setting with a result on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6). It measures no pretraining loss, fits no power law and does no allocation sweep, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that ICL benefits from larger models, especially for temporal normalization. Fine-tuning (notably LoRA) improves over ICL, but gains plateau or degrade beyond 2.8B and above 6B, which they call inverse scaling from overfitting on a moderate, imbalanced and partly duplicated dataset. They suggest 410M balances capacity and generalization, and that data quality and augmentation can matter more than scale.
record.recipe_differences: This study evaluates task-specific deidentification and temporal-normalization performance across model sizes; it does not use the original scaling-law loss-fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by task, model size, and adaptation method (ICL, full fine-tuning, or LoRA). The authors also report sensitivity to training-set duplication and to the number and deduplication of ICL examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning beats ICL below 2.8B but not above 6B. LoRA beats full fine-tuning for >1B models, and 70M-LoRA underperforms.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of fine-tuning over ICL shrinks or reverses with model size on small task datasets.

record.problems: The main text gives some qualitative comparisons but most per-model scores are in figures or supplementary tables not included here. Evaluation is on pathology-report deidentification and temporal normalization, not held-out pretraining loss; the authors also note a moderate, imbalanced dataset and possible duplication-related sensitivity.
record.rows_left_out: Competition leaderboard scores and team-method comparisons, including reported data-augmentation results, were not extracted because they do not provide a systematic model-size comparison relevant to V6. Fig. 4 comparisons of ICL example counts and deduplicated examples were also left out because they do not test scale predictability.

untested.parts: Predictability: no fitted trend and no extrapolation. Performance is not related to pretraining loss. Only two tasks in a single domain.
All; fine-tuning is studied, but no power-law form is tested.

missing.what: Per-model ICL and fine-tuned F1 values across all eight Pythia sizes; only figure and supplementary values exist.
Point values at two sizes: Pythia-410M-LoRA macro-F 0.791/0.695, Pythia-2.8B-ICL 0.621/0.362, and Pythia-2.8B LoRA 0.764/0.650.
Authors state the 410M model strikes the best capacity/generalization balance.

record.verdict_notes: The tranche is T3 (new downstream setting), not T2. The reader's r1, r2 and r5–r8 compare against the competition average or between adaptation methods, not across sizes, so they are unlinked. Hoffmann et al. is cited only in passing. Participant results (e.g. Ru et al.: more Pythia parameters helped under QLoRA) are cited results and should not be rows.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute relationship is measured.
No loss-law fit or prediction of larger-run loss from smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token counts.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture at a fixed parameter count.
No power-law loss test in other modalities or training regimes.

Measures task-specific deidentification and temporal-normalization F1 across Pythia sizes and methods, not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; it does not establish a general relationship across downstream tasks.
The study discusses effects of dataset size, duplication, and fine-tuning on task performance, but does not test loss-law exponents, compute-optimal allocations, or fit-method dependence.

rows.subject: Pythia models with more than 1 B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared few-shot ICL task performance across Pythia model sizes.
rows.baseline: Average performance of all competition submissions
rows.value: Performed comparably to the average performance of all submissions; plotted scores are figure only.
rows.note: The text gives a grouped comparison for models above 1 B, not individual scores for each model.
rows.check: Grouped comparison of >1B models against the competition average. It does not show how performance changes with size, so it cannot show the scaling effect.

rows.subject: Pythia-160 M
rows.operation_detail: Compared few-shot ICL task performance across Pythia model sizes.
rows.value: Performance was described as close to the average; plotted score is figure only.
rows.note: The article does not provide the exact score in the main text.
rows.check: A single model (160M) compared with the competition average macro-F1. This is not a scale trend.

rows.subject: Pythia models of varying sizes
rows.size_stated: 70 M, 160 M, 410 M, 1 B, 1.4 B, 2.8 B, 6.9 B, and 12 B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared few-shot ICL task performance across the Pythia model suite.
rows.value: Models with at least 1.4 B parameters reached micro/macro F1 above 0.30/0.15; models with at least 2.8 B reached macro-F1 above 0.32. The top-ranked model was 6.9 B; plotted scores are figure only.
rows.note: The article reports size thresholds and the best model, rather than a single monotonic trend.
rows.check: F1 thresholds rise with size (≥1.4B, ≥2.8B), but the best Subtask 2 model is 6.9B, not 12B. The trend is not monotonic.

source_check.locator_found: Results, In-context learning performance; Fig. 3; lines 229–267. Subtask 2 requires at least 1.4B for micro/macro-F1 >0.30/0.15 and at least 2.8B for macro-F1 >0.32; 6.9B performs best.

rows.subject: Pythia-12 B
rows.operation_detail: Compared few-shot ICL task performance across Pythia model sizes.
rows.baseline: Other tested Pythia sizes; exact reference value not stated
rows.value: The 12 B model was the best-performing model; plotted scores are figure only.
rows.note: The text identifies the best model but does not state its numerical F1 scores.
rows.check: The largest model (12B) is best on Subtask 1 ICL. Only the ranking is stated; scores are in Fig. 3.

source_check.locator_found: Results, In-context learning performance; Fig. 3; lines 243–264. The text identifies 12B as best for Subtask 1 without numerical F1 scores.

rows.subject: Pythia models with fewer than 2.8 B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned Pythia models and compared their task performance with ICL.
rows.measure: F1; recall rates also described as improved
rows.value: Fine-tuned models showed notable performance improvement over ICL; exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The grouped result is stated for models below 2.8 B.
rows.check: Compares fine-tuning with ICL, an adaptation-method comparison, not a scale comparison.

rows.subject: Pythia-70 M-LoRA
rows.operation_detail: Compared LoRA fine-tuning performance with ICL and full fine-tuning.
rows.value: Underperformed its counterparts; exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The text explicitly identifies this as the exception to the reported fine-tuning improvements.
rows.check: LoRA vs ICL/full fine-tuning at 70M is a method comparison. 'Reversed' is not a state relative to any version.

rows.subject: Pythia models with more than 6 B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared full fine-tuning with ICL across model sizes.
rows.value: The full-fine-tuning advantage over ICL was not significant; exact plotted scores are figure only.
rows.note: The article does not provide a statistical test or p-value for the stated non-significant advantage.
rows.check: Full fine-tuning vs ICL above 6B is a method comparison, not scale.

rows.subject: Pythia models with more than 6 B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared fine-tuned performance with ICL across model sizes.
rows.value: Macro-F1 was lower than with ICL; exact plotted scores are figure only.
rows.note: The article reports this decline for models above 6 B parameters.
rows.check: Fine-tuned vs ICL macro-F1 above 6B is a method comparison. The size trend is captured in r9 and r10.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8 B
rows.operation_detail: Compared task performance across fine-tuned Pythia model sizes.
rows.baseline: Other tested Pythia sizes; exact reference value not stated
rows.value: The authors state that performance was optimal at 2.8 B; micro-F1 peaked there with full fine-tuning, while macro-F1 declined as model size increased. Exact scores are figure only.
rows.note: The reported optimum and the differing micro- and macro-F1 trends qualify a simple scale-performance relationship.
rows.check: Under full fine-tuning, micro-F peaks at 2.8B, while the text says macro-F declined as model size increased. Improvement with scale holds only up to a point, and is reversed for macro-F.

source_check.locator_found: Fig. 5 caption and accompanying results, lines 281–315; Discussion, lines 925–936. The stated optimum is 2.8B; full-fine-tuning micro-F peaks there, whereas macro-F declines with increasing size.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8 B
rows.operation_detail: Compared task performance across fine-tuned Pythia model sizes.
rows.baseline: Other tested Pythia sizes; exact reference value not stated
rows.value: The authors state that performance was optimal at 2.8 B and plateaued or deteriorated beyond this point for fine-tuning approaches; exact scores are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes plateauing or degradation beyond 2.8 B, including lower macro-F1 than ICL for models above 6 B.
rows.check: Fine-tuned performance improves up to 2.8B, then plateaus (LoRA) or deteriorates (full fine-tuning). Fig. 5 notes a crossover between 70M and 160M.

source_check.locator_found: Fig. 5 caption and accompanying results, lines 281–315; Fine-tuning performance, lines 317–328. Both subtasks have a stated 2.8B optimum, followed by LoRA plateauing or full-fine-tuning deterioration; Subtask 2 full-fine-tuning macro-F1 falls below ICL above 6B.

relationships.condition: Pretrained Pythia with 5-shot kNN-selected ICL, both subtasks
relationships.reason: Subtask 2 F1 thresholds are reached only at ≥1.4B and ≥2.8B, and the 12B model is best on Subtask 1 (r3, r4). Gains are not strictly monotonic: 6.9B is best on Subtask 2 (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Subtask 2 F1 thresholds were reached only at ≥1.4B and ≥2.8B, while 12B performed best on Subtask 1 and 6.9B on Subtask 2.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pythia models below 2.8 B parameters and the reported best-sized ICL models
reader_labels.reason: Task scores generally improved with fine-tuning below 2.8 B, and the best ICL systems were the 12 B model for Subtask 1 and 6.9 B model for Subtask 2 (r1, r3, r4, r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Fine-tuned Pythia models at larger sizes, particularly above 6 B
reader_labels.reason: The reported advantage is not consistent across methods or tasks: 70 M LoRA underperformed, the full-tuning advantage was not significant for Subtask 1 above 6 B, and Subtask 2 macro-F1 fell below ICL above 6 B (r6, r7, r8, r9, r10).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Fine-tuned models above 6 B on Subtask 2 macro-F1
reader_labels.reason: For these models, macro-F1 was lower than the corresponding ICL result, contrary to a consistent improvement with increasing scale (r8).
